subtype: Approach: finding out what each plant needs [Thinking]
passage: Note from Nilesh at the plant nursery. A boy of about ten, Ojas, came in on Saturday and asked what each of his two seedlings needs. I told him chilli wants plenty of sun and mint does better in the shade. He had forgotten his notebook, so he wrote it on his palm. "So chilli by the window and mint next to the wall," he said. I nodded. On Tuesday he came back with a photo of both pots in their places and asked if that was right. It was. - Nilesh

qa.q: Where did Ojas write down what he learned?
qa.a: He wrote it on his palm.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he came back with the photo on Tuesday?
qa.a: Eager and a little unsure whether he was right, but proud enough to show his work.

qa.q: What else could Ojas do to check the plants get the right light, and why?
qa.a: He could watch the pots over several days and move them if the leaves look pale or burnt, because plants show what they need.

qa.q: How does Nilesh see Ojas's return visit?
qa.a: Nilesh is pleased and encouraging, since Nilesh confirms it was right and notes the boy's interest.

grounding: A boy asks a nursery worker what each plant needs and places his pots by the window and the wall accordingly.

subtype: Approach: finding out what each plant needs [Thinking]
passage:
Sunday
Today Nikita-didi took me to the nursery near the flyover because my chilli plant looked sad and my mint was going brown. I asked the nursery uncle why. He asked, "Where are they?" I said, "Both behind the curtain in my room." He laughed. "Chilli is a sun plant. Mint likes shade and wet feet." On the way home I thought about our flat like a map. The kitchen window gets sun all morning, so that's for the chilli. The balcony corner beside the wall stays shady and cool, so that's for the mint. I moved both pots as soon as we got home. I'll check in a week to see if I was right.
Divyansh

qa.q: Where did Divyansh put the chilli?
qa.a: By the kitchen window, which gets sun all morning.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel about the plants before the visit?
qa.a: Divyansh was worried that the chilli looked sad and the mint was going brown.

qa.q: What else could Divyansh do to test the new spots?
qa.a: Divyansh could note how the leaves look each day for a week, so it is clear whether the move helped.

qa.q: How might the nursery uncle see Divyansh's question?
qa.a: He laughed, amused at the curtain, but answered kindly, perhaps pleased that a child asked.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child learning what each plant needs from a nursery worker and placing the pots to match.

subtype: Approach: finding out what each plant needs [Thinking]
passage: At the Thursday haat in their kasba, Saurabh found Vijay-bhaiya's nursery stall between the bangle sellers and the potato heaps. He had two saplings in a cloth bag: a chilli from his aunt and a mint cutting from school. "Where should these go? Our courtyard is small." Vijay-bhaiya squinted at the plants. "Chilli wants sun from morning to afternoon. Mint wants shade and damp. Keep them apart." Walking home, Saurabh pictured the courtyard: the sunny patch by the tulsi platform, the cool corner by the handpump where the neem throws shade. That evening he set the chilli in a pot on the sunny side and planted the mint by the handpump, where splashes would keep it damp.

qa.a: Between the bangle sellers and the potato heaps at the Thursday haat.

qa.q: What was Saurabh thinking on the walk home?
qa.a: He felt curious and pleased, picturing the courtyard to match each plant's need.

qa.q: What else could Saurabh try if the mint still struggles?
qa.a: He could move it again or ask Vijay-bhaiya on the next haat day, bringing a leaf to show.

qa.q: How might Vijay-bhaiya feel about being asked?
qa.a: He seems glad to help, giving clear, simple advice to a boy who wants to get it right.

grounding: A boy asks a nursery seller what each plant needs and places the chilli in sun and the mint in shade.
